news.summary_en: Silicon Valley is increasingly defining 'taste' as the ultimate human moat against generative AI's algorithmic slop. The current industry debate centers on whether aesthetic judgment is merely a pattern-matching exercise achievable by LLMs, or a uniquely human cognitive capability that determines future market valuation of creative output.
paragraphs: To move through A.I.-era San Francisco as a relatively normal person is to confront the sheer volume of bewildering concepts that tech has lately thrust upon us. Looking at billboards and bus ads, you gather that agentic virtual agents are here, and that something called “sharded Postgres” is here, too. You learn that inference is more than just vibes, and even more inscrutably, that ▲ ~/ npm i ai. Rather than give yourself a headache trying to parse these ciphers, you might feel tempted to ignore them entirely: not my lingo, not my problem. But a nagging dread lingers. What if all that gibberish portends irreversible changes already in the process of reshaping our lives? What if agentic agents really are here, and what if none of us can opt out of the future they’re ushering in?

Recently, lots of people who work in tech — and lots of us who don’t but feel forced to think about it anyway — have faced disquieting questions about what computers are capable of. Near the top of the list is whether they’ll achieve superintelligence, turn malevolent and bring about the apocalypse. More fun to mull, as dystopian musings go, is another newly burning question: whether computers can learn taste.

“Taste” became an unlikely tech buzzword this year, invoked and debated in essays and X posts by founders, investors, engineers and other would-be Silicon Valley oracles. We’ve long understood taste, in its simplest terms, as a capacity for judgment that certain people possess in uncommon degrees. Someone with taste can behold a made thing (a song, an outfit, a living room) and deftly evaluate its relationship to an ever-shifting set of aesthetic rules and cultural conventions. Because computers currently lack this capacity — and because much of what generative A.I. produces today is of such abysmal quality that we’ve adopted the pejorative “slop” to describe it — some in the industry have come to see taste as a sort of market differentiator for humanity itself.

They tout taste as a “new core skill.” They hail it as a “moat,” protecting us from our theoretical robot usurpers whose output will never be as “net new and resonant” as ours. Others counter that computers are pretty good at learning rules, and predict that sufficiently sophisticated models will one day cross the moat and learn to be tasteful, too. “One by one,” an A.I. founder told Fast Company, “the things that we were sure were uniquely human just turn out to be patterns the models can learn.”

There are obvious philosophical dimensions to this debate. For tech bosses, there may be a psychological dimension too. Silicon Valley has created the first class of elites in history whom we associate with taste’s utter absence. If you’re among this class, the sense that a pesky humanities blind spot occludes your all-seeing STEM vision may irk you. If you’re a company like OpenAI, which recently put out a streetwear drop in a clumsy play for Supreme-style cool, you may dream of merchandising the blind spot away. If you’re someone like Mark Zuckerberg, currently engaged in a highly publicized wardrobe pivot toward Prada loafers and knits from the Row, you may dream of shopping it away.

Above all, if you are an A.I. true believer, you may dream of engineering it away. A.I. labs have been expending enormous resources to try and teach their models how to tell the ineffably good from the ineffably bad. A multibillion-dollar A.I. subindustry has emerged, in which start-ups throw ungodly sums at legions of freelancers, hiring them to critique A.I. output across various creative endeavors, like writing, music and VFX. In July, one such company, Mercor, was reportedly shelling out more than $4 million daily to 30,000 contractors. As of last month, according to “60 Minutes,” that number had swelled to more than 100,000.

It’s possible that the most significant outcome of such efforts will not be to make generative models any more “tasteful” but to funnel an obscene amount of A.I. funny money into the coffers of well-positioned players. Yet the moonshot goal at the big A.I. labs remains to develop a technology that can automate every conceivable kind of labor — not just the task-driven, white-collar labor of paralegals but more abstract creative labor too. Hence the emphasis on taste.

If Silicon Valley seems short on taste these days, it’s because until now, basically no tech companies cared about tastefulness, save one: Apple. Steve Jobs was a refined showman who owned black Issey Miyake mocknecks in multiple. His longtime lead industrial designer, Jony Ive, was an avowed admirer of Dieter Rams. Together they developed a sleek array of devices, including the iMac and iPhone. But other industry behemoths aren’t in the business of selling high-end consumer goods, and so they’ve tended to build themselves around coders like Zuckerberg, who as a cohort aren’t known for their interest in squishy intangibles.

“To me, taste is by definition fabulously subjective, and fabulously human,” Jony Ive told me recently. This might help explain why taste can stymie engineers, supply-chain machers and other corporate number-crunchers who worship at the altar of hard data. “There’s a tendency for people to be more comfortable talking about issues you can measure easily,” he says.

The truly vexing thing is that taste isn’t Silicon Valley’s bugbear alone. Thanks to its creations, the ways in which all of us relate to our preferences have undergone immensely alienating changes. We discover favorite songs listening to playlists created by machines, we develop “personal style” watching TikTok influencers, we rate movies on Letterboxd to generate engagement from strangers. We go to our feeds to figure out what to like and how to be.

As we scroll, we fear miring ourselves in algorithmic loops where the total possible field of “what we can ever like” draws only from the digital heap of “what we have liked before.” Even interests that would have once registered as arcane, we can now compress into knowing “starter pack”-style memes, which taxonomize the putative taste markers of subcultural costumes (Chinati souvenir cap, Rachel Cusk novel, Dashwood Books tote, matcha latte). The implication is that any set of tastes can be reduced to a playbook. Or, if you like, to a piece of code.

In 1961, the literary theorist René Girard argued that people like what they like because they see others liking it. He called this “mimetic desire.” Today, in our online panopticon of constant surveillance and self-presentation, our preferences are liable to feel less our own than ever.

A.I. promises only to compound this. Many of us have already begun turning to chatbots not just to replace human interactions but also to do our thinking for us, creating what even OpenAI has acknowledged is a danger of “social deskilling.” It adds up to a moment of unprecedented unease around taste, so pronounced as to feel existential. What will we like, and who will it make us, when we come out the other side?

Human beings have felt anxiety about taste as long as we’ve had the concept. A 19th-century French count takes pride in his exquisite Beauvais tapestries until a cooler count comes by and won’t shut up about his Gobelins. These nobles’ grandchildren sneer at the gauche industrialist filling garages with flashy cars, and he sneers back at the fading gentry’s threadbare rugs. A 1980s commodities broker flashes his Patek at the maître d’ in hopes of scoring a better table. The sculptor with whom the broker’s wife is having an affair thinks fancy watches are the compensatory pastime of philistine goobers. A 2026 creative director posts a picture of that sculptor’s monograph on an Aalto stool, impressing some and inspiring others to roll their eyes at the obviousness of the tableau. Taste is a means of judging the world that has long created a means for the world to judge you.

We once understood taste primarily as a function of aristocratic wealth and “good breeding.” It wasn’t until the 1920s that a disruptive new figure was born — the modern consumer — and with it a new, more putatively democratic concept of taste. Until that point, unless you were a leisure-class elite, you only bought new shoes when you wore out your old pair. But with interwar production lines booming, advertisers set about crafting a “new and essential message,” as the filmmaker Adam Curtis puts it in his 2002 documentary “The Century of the Self”: “you bought things not just for need but to express your inner sense of yourself to others.”

Conveniently for manufacturers, this inner sense was far more chasmic than any pair of shoes could ever satisfy: An infinite market, defined by our urges, aspirations, insecurities, vanities and tastes, sprawled within each and every one of us. The counterculture pushed back against this annexed vision of the self in the 1960s, rejecting consumerism as an arm of the capitalist-imperialist war machine it sought to topple. But that energy was eventually redirected into the free-market-amenable pursuit of “self-actualization.” Seekers were assured that selfishness was, in fact, anything but, because the best way to improve society was to focus on improving yourself. The result was a generation of post-counterculture consumers who insisted on buying only what Adam Curtis calls “products that would express their individuality, their difference in a conformist world.”

It was here that the lines between identity, consumption and taste got severely scrambled. Having anti-consumerist inclinations didn’t have to mean rejecting consumerism. It just meant buying products “aligned” with your “values.” By the 1980s, the advertising industry had coined an indelible term for the canniest approach to dividing and conquering customers: “lifestyle marketing.”

Four decades later, those lines feel harder than ever to separate. Streaming Agnès Varda films on Criterion and watching inane, Sephora-sponsored “Get Ready With Me” reels on Instagram are muddled into a single act: “content consumption.” Everything we do online and, increasingly, offline, accumulates into dossiers about us that data brokers sell to advertisers. Lifestyle marketing is so complete that today we aren’t just our own markets but our own marketers, too, pressured to steward our “personal brands.”

This can take bluntly literal forms. Friends trading recommendations on social media, and even in private group chats, have started to share affiliate links, which entitle them to kickbacks if those tips lead to purchases. As the journalist Kathryn Jezer-Morton puts it in her book “The Story of Your Life,” about the warping effects of social media on consciousness, we’ve come to see ourselves as “little entrepreneurs of selfhood.”
The things we like, the things we buy, even moments of friendship — all can represent sales opportunities.

When it comes to taste, much of our discomfort has long boiled down to a single question: Did my preference arise organically from somewhere within me, or was it implanted, artificially and insidiously, from without? This dilemma has always been crazy-making because it depends on a false binary. Taste, like language, is irreducibly social. It can never exist in some vacuum of pure interiority. What’s different now is that the internet has created a vast asymmetry between the internal and the external. We’ve dissolved the boundary between living our lives and representing them online, and the ramifications for taste are dizzying.
“Taste is a means of judging the world that has long created a means for the world to judge you.”

“Instagram has been one of the most incredible media platforms ever for showing taste and broadcasting it to the world,” says W. David Marx, author of the 2022 book “Status and Culture.” “But the very medium distorts and devalues the flex as it’s happening, because there’s no subtlety to it. The thing about taste is, it’s supposed to be behavioral residue — these signals are supposed to be part of your life, not something you intentionally aspire to signal. But the internet makes it almost impossible to tell the difference.”

In tracing the genealogies of our tastes, we could once point with more confidence to seeming gold-standard factors like organic discovery, time spent digging and serendipity. Online, though, the cultivation of taste can feel less like a process of messy chance and more like updates we download on schedule. I thought wearing muted earth tones when everyone was wearing loud prints was my idea, until I picked up my phone and saw 20 people in earth tones, too.

“I remember seeing all these memes in the past few years about being able to judge someone’s screen time” — how many hours they spend on their phone — “by the outfit they were wearing,” says Biz Sherbert, who co-hosts the podcast “Nymphet Alumni” and writes the newsletter “American Style,” which focus on youth-culture trends. “That felt really depressing to me. Not because I couldn’t believe people were getting references from the internet but because people had developed this kind of taste paranoia.”

Taste paranoia isn’t exactly new. People have long filled bookshelves with books they haven’t read — impersonators fetishizing objects of distinction to flatter their self-image and impress houseguests. But as we articulate our public selves online, the opportunities for impersonation multiply. And so, while we’ve always been prone to some confusion about our own motivations, and to some mistrust of others’, today we’re more confused and mistrustful than ever. We fear liking the wrong things, or liking the right things the wrong way: We fret about appearing “performative” in the books we read, accuse others of perpetrating “cosplay” in the clothes they wear and dismiss legions more as mere “N.P.C.s.” — automatons following trends in lock step, like “non-playable characters” in video games.

Secretly we might worry we have more N.P.C. tendencies in ourselves than we care to admit. When we get meager likes on a pic of a Noguchi lamp, we wonder: Are our friends too “basic” in their tastes to get it? Or were we too basic to know to buy an Ingo Maurer instead?

Talking with Sherbert, who is 29, I was struck by the fact that she identified “the biggest driver” in the development of her own taste as Tumblr, an image-heavy blogging platform that reached peak popularity during her pre-algorithmic, early-2010s adolescence. Tumblr has long since been supplanted in the zeitgeist by other image-heavy platforms, like Instagram and TikTok, but it has played a sneakily pivotal role in rewriting the workings of taste as we know them.

On the one hand, it was a place ripe with discoveries: “It’s where you saw the screenshot of a Sofia Coppola movie, then went and watched your first Sofia Coppola movie,” Sherbet said. And since your feed consisted entirely of images from people you chose to follow, it felt like an active reflection of your own taste. In hindsight, though, Tumblr’s most consequential feature was the way it let such “discovery” happen at a marked remove from “context.” Someone you followed reblogged a picture that someone else had reblogged after someone else reblogged it, daisy-chaining back to a hard-to-identify original poster who’d scanned in the image from … well, that could be tough to know, too.

Particularly curious and determined users like Sherbert could go deeper and sleuth out answers, but by and large the site became synonymous with a base-line level of epistemological disorientation. Learning the details of any picture’s origins came second to the narcotic experience of letting vibey imagery wash over you, in a provenance-dissolving logic that has come to characterize much of our scrolling today. “WHAT IS THIS?” a gag T-shirt featuring the cover art of Joy Division’s 1979 album, “Unknown Pleasures,” asked several years ago. “I’VE SEEN IT ON TUMBLR.”

Today, in the algorithmically organized climate of taste paranoia Sherbert describes, any group that forms around shared cultural interests — amateur film photography, midcentury-modern Brazilian furniture, artisanal Japanese clothing — can be derided as its own little herd of sheep, grazing their own subsection of the same predictive pasture we’ve all been fenced into.

Are there gaps in the fences we might wiggle through? Perhaps I’m committing the fallacy of “romanticizing the way things were when I was 15,” but I think there are clues hiding in the last decade of life humans knew before the internet changed everything, which also happens to be the decade when I turned 15: the 1990s.

When I was in high school, I saw a classmate wearing a green T-shirt decorated with a photo of a crocheted doll. Two words flanked its face: “Sonic Youth.” This classmate played in a band with older kids and he had a “suffer no fools” aura I found intimidating. It was 1994. Sonic Youth was a legendary New York City noise-rock band, and the tee captured the cover of “Dirty,” their 1992 album.

Not that I knew this at the time. Maybe I’d seen Kurt Cobain mention Sonic Youth in a magazine, but I had no idea what they sounded like. Still, their name seemed cool, the shirt looked cool and its owner was cool, so — in an act of raw mimetic desire — I made it my conscious mission to like Sonic Youth.

This was a multistep, multiyear process. In a later era, I could have watched their top-viewed videos on YouTube, bought a T-shirt and declared myself a fan. But in the ’90s, that would have incurred an untenable social penalty: “You were scared of being called a ‘poser,’” David Marx said when I told him this story, invoking the silver-bullet insult of the era.

Instead, I had to save up for a cassette of “Dirty” (CDs were out of my budget), find a shop that stocked it and then grapple with the alarming discovery, when I actually listened to the album, that I found much of the music strange and unpleasant. I was a kid, with little frame of reference for what Sonic Youth were doing, but I stuck with it, sensing that some important epiphany awaited me on the other side of my discomfort.

I listened to the band with friends, making sense of choices that excited and flummoxed us. I read music criticism in The Village Voice, noted which bands were on the Lollapalooza lineup alongside Sonic Youth and which bands’ posters were tacked up beside theirs at record stores. In halting, uncertain steps, I situated my interest in the band within a broader world, working my way toward an appreciation that felt deeper and more personal.

With time, Sonic Youth became a base camp for further explorations. Who was Mike Kelley, the artist behind the doll on the “Dirty” cover? Who was Glenn Branca, the downtown composer whose guitar squalls, a friend informed me, had inspired Sonic Youth’s? Who was Steve Reich, the minimalist legend whose undulating figures had influenced Branca? What sublime mysteries would knowing all these answers unlock?

When I try to recall how my tastes formed, pre-internet, this is where my mind goes. I think about how my ’90s adolescence corresponded with the brief dominance of Gen-X values: a concerted effort to resuscitate a defiant countercultural position after the crass reign of ’80s yuppiedom, prizing the holdout over the sellout, the obscure over the obvious, the difficult over the easy.

I also think about how my naked desire to like something cool, counterbalanced by my dread of peer scorn, forced me to devote elaborate effort to the ostensibly simple goal of “telling people I liked Sonic Youth.” And how, at a certain point, like any novice working toward competence, I felt I’d actively earned my taste.

This is not how things have worked for a while. For starters, we’re inclined to remember ’90s Gen X-ers as annoying people with archaic values about purity. Their unapologetically materialistic archnemeses, the yuppies, have, for the moment anyway, triumphed.

What’s more, earning something requires time and sustained attention, and that’s not how anyone would characterize contemporary life’s cadence. As often as not, we look at our screens to let meaningless information inundate us in a semi-aware haze, or to get specific answers instantly. If we see, say, Kylie Jenner wearing a vintage Sonic Youth shirt in a paparazzi shot, we can just buy a repro on Depop. The social internet is a supernova of context collapse, with no penalties for taking shortcuts. Assembling your identity need not be very different from assembling a mood board.

This has a certain liberatory aspect, along the lines of “we can be whomever we choose.” But it can also leave us feeling unsatisfied and anchorless. And in our milieu of frictionless efficiency, we’ve started to sense that something valuable is getting lost. “I think it really builds your self-esteem to solve a problem,” Sherbert said. “That’s why there’s benefits to children playing sports — it’s good to fall and get back up again, in whatever you do.”
What if we conceive of taste, then, as an immensely valuable skill for tackling a problem, the problem being: How do we come to know other people, and come to know ourselves, better?

Taste, after all, is what steers us toward culture that’s not merely pleasurable, not merely flattering to our self-image and advantageous to our social standing, but rich in meaning too. This culture can thrill us even as it confounds us, putting us on unfamiliar terrain where we glimpse the subjectivities of others, and broaden our own.

Crucially, taste leads us to other people, and for all its exclusionary uses, it has an essentially pro-social function. Exclusion is a necessary part of this, because it’s important to be able to draw a line between an “us,” defined by values we find ennobling, and a “them,” defined by values we find abhorrent, or at least banal. When we talk about finishing a great book and “running outside to tell somebody,” going to a concert and “finding our tribe,” meeting someone who hates the same popular thing we hate and “feeling less insane” or watching a beautiful film and “feeling less alone,” this is what we’re saying. Taste is a rumble in me that comes into phase with a rumble in you.

For a time i t was possible to see life online as amplifying the rumblings. We were sold a dream of the internet as a place of unprecedented connection. But over the last decade or so, this technology of interconnectedness has combined with shifting social conditions to make us feel profoundly lonely. In the process, something vital about the way we relate to our taste — which is to say, the way we relate to ourselves and to other people — has been damaged. Is there any reason to believe A.I. won’t make things worse?

A few short years ago, an outlandish, sci-fi-flavored premise began circulating that, in retrospect, gets to the heart of how A.I. is changing things. Known as the Dead Internet Theory, this premise emerged around 2020, proposing that most seemingly human activity we encountered on the web was actually the work of bots pretending to be humans. We thought we still traveled an internet dominated by real people like us, but real people were few and far between — stray ghosts haunting a machine.

This theory caught on because it captured what online life was starting to feel like. Today, as the internet teems with A.I.-generated Google results, A.I. customer-service agents, A.I. influencers shilling medical advice, malicious swarms of A.I. hackers and A.I. possums who can do tricks on A.I. skateboards, the notion of a Dead Internet has gone from sci-fi to plain fact: This June, the web-hosting giant Cloudflare announced that bots now represent nearly 60 percent of all web traffic.

Properly speaking, the Dead Internet Theory describes an undead internet. There is something inherently necrotic about A.I., designed as it is to feed on, regurgitate and reanimate the entire corpus of human culture in the form of weird digital corpse-flesh. This helps account for the queasy feeling that A.I.-generated culture can provoke in us. What’s more, A.I. feeds on itself, creating new corpse-flesh from old in an inbred dynamic that researchers at Microsoft internally described as a “doom loop.” None of which, it goes without saying, is a very tasteful thing to do. (The Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft for copyright infringement, which the companies deny.)

A personalized-entertainment extrapolation on the Dead Internet Theory in a scenario where computers have learned taste would look something like this: Imagine logging on to some future version of Netflix and finding a selection of high-quality entertainment produced just for you. Say you’re a fan of the sui generis comedian Tim Robinson. Imagine prompting the platform to generate a new season of “I Think You Should Leave,” Robinson’s beloved cult sketch series. “Make the six episodes Tim Robinson would make if he brought the show back today,” you might say, “with contemporary references and jokes that capture the best parts of his sensibility without ever feeling like old, warmed-over Tim Robinson.”

Imagine the platform quickly creating thousands of would-be skits, and thousands more simulated viewers to appraise them, taking their feedback into account, narrowing the options and serving up your request. Computationally speaking, this model would be capable not only of mining past data to identify and replicate patterns but also of extrapolating on and departing from those patterns in nuanced, satisfyingly unpredictable, functionally tasteful ways.

“That’s the full A.G.I.-pilled version,” Joey Flynn, a veteran tech product designer, said, when I put this hypothetical to him. He was invoking the theoretical state of so-called Artificial General Intelligence, when, as he put it, “whatever insight you would have, the model can have. It has so much information, it knows when it’s time to flip the script.”

Flynn, who has held positions high up at companies including OpenAI and Instagram, is among many A.I. enthusiasts prone to regard A.G.I. as a pipe dream — “Easier said than done,” he said. Perhaps it’s no coincidence that he also has taste, and that, as it happens, he never planned on a career in tech at all. Facebook hired Flynn straight out of college in 2009, even though he had no product-design education, and none as a coder. He studied Bauhaus principles and Swiss typography, imagining a life creating fonts. When I first met him, at a party in San Francisco in 2021, he wore a faded old Stone Island jacket, crunchy Keen sandals and a vintage Cartier Tank: nothing tech-bro about it. He designed an anorak in collaboration with an influential Manhattan men’s wear shop, and helped some friends open a loud, sweaty, beloved wine bar in San Francisco.

That same year he founded a company with two prominent machine-learning engineers he had befriended at Instagram, which OpenAI later bought, intent on bringing the trio into its ranks. Flynn was tasked with crafting an interface for the generative-video tool Sora, which turned prompts (“a dragon fighting a shark in space”) into realistic clips.

When I asked Flynn what he thought was driving Silicon Valley’s taste obsession, he put it in practical terms. If a bunch of different people give an A.I. model “the same prompt, like, ‘Make an app that looks like it was designed by Apple,’” he explained, “it’s basically going to give us the same output. So when you hear people saying it’s all about taste now, I think it’s: Who are the people with some insight to where they can guide the model into doing something more resonant?” Jony Ive echoed this line of thinking. He told me that he and the designers he employs at his company, LoveFrom, incorporate unreleased OpenAI models into their practice, which allows them to “spend less time trying to embody an idea” — but “the primary tool I use,” he said, remains “my pencil and my sketchbook.”

In tech jargon, someone who uses technology to enhance his powers is known as a “centaur”: human actor up top, software boosting his capabilities from down below. Riffing on this image, the author Cory Doctorow has written about a distressing shadow figure called the “reverse centaur,” where the human is reduced to a mere appendage, toiling in technology’s service. Amazon drivers, electronically monitored down to the movements of their pupils, are totemic reverse centaurs. With generative A.I. — a technology whose “allegiances,” as it were, are split between us, its owners and, most murkily, itself — it can be tricky to say who is ultimately in control. It can be tough, that is, to tell one kind of centaur from the other.
“The social internet is a supernova of context collapse, with no penalties for taking shortcuts.”

When we prompt an A.I. model to produce better work, in the way Flynn describes, there is a disconcerting sense in which we’re acting as unwitting reverse centaurs, actively training our would-be replacements. While scrolling the Mercor site, I saw a listing for design experts to train A.I. models. Isn’t the tech bosses’ dream, I asked Flynn, to reach the point where their models get so good they can eliminate you?

“I don’t know that I’d use the word ‘eliminate,’” he said. “It’s more: Can we triple the output of a human? That’s what we’re already seeing, where now an engineer isn’t writing code all day, they’re just controlling a fleet of agents and having them do 100 times the work they could do before.” Flynn was referring to so-called vibe coding, where programmers and laypeople alike can ask A.I. to build programs for them using plain-English prompts.

Of course, we tend to seek fundamentally different things from culture than we do from code, and there’s something deeply unsettling about the notion of “vibe crafted” culture, produced prompt by prompt by a centaur auteur.

Among creative people who don’t work in tech, generative A.I. seems broadly unpopular. But it does have some thoughtful converts. An experimental music producer who goes by the name Lil Internet has talked about trying to “crack” popular music-making A.I. tools like Udio and Suno in the pursuit of sounds that emerge “out of the triangulation of, like, 800 points in machine space.” On the music podcast “No Tags,” Lil Internet cautioned against dismissing all A.I. as a priori slop. “There’s a huge spam problem with A.I., of course,” he said. “But short-form video itself, the entire physics of TikTok, is just this brain-hacking thing without A.I. content, right?” The worst A.I. slop, he ventured, is simply “an intensification.”

Intensification is a great way to understand lots of the A.I. output we encounter today. Insipid therapy speak, dumb novelty songs, fast-fashion churn, bludgeoningly incoherent action sequences, cynical recombinations of existing I.P. — A.I. didn’t invent any of these. It’s just extremely good at reproducing them, and other addictive modes of pre-existing junk culture, inexpensively and at near-infinite scale.

Earlier this year, OpenAI announced it was shutting down Sora, its video-generating model. Not long after, Flynn left the company. But at a time when video clips, with their direct pipelines to our lizard brains, are busy devouring all other forms of media, this seems like an isolated hiccup rather than some broader indicator.

Generative A.I. will most likely continue to thrive in intrinsically tasteless contexts, where the only thing that matters is maximizing attention and minimizing cost. Absent-mindedly scrolling X not long ago, I was served a grainy surveillance video in which a bumbling armed man barges into a store. His gun flies comically out of his hand and, failing to hop the counter to retrieve it, he does a 180 and jump-kicks the door, at which point his pants fall down.

I didn’t know if it was real. Ultimately it made no difference. I let it loop three times, contemplating it like an idiot koan, and as my life force dwindled, someone, somewhere, made some money. The writer Aidan Walker calls this “slop capitalism.”

New attempts at elite connoisseurship may well emerge in this mind-numbing landscape. Susan Sontag famously argued for the “good taste of bad taste,” and how ironically distanced enjoyment of campy mass culture could become its own form of discernment. Perhaps an erudite class of would-be sloptimists will arise, with their own neo-camp strategies for separating “good” A.I. trash from “bad” A.I. trash.

But with enough time and exposure, A.I. output might shed its uncanny telltales altogether, frustrating such moves. Children raised on A.I.-generated YouTube animations and other jabbering brain-rot content might be primed to accept so-called synthetic culture, along with synthetic companionship, on its ever-more-humanlike face.

We can already see a sort of Chatbot Canon of Taste beginning to assemble itself. This year, a young social media strategist named Cait Cavell helped conduct an informal “A.I. shopping experiment” that doubled as an A.I. taste test. She prompted seven different A.I. models to recommend “the perfect white T-shirt,” “the best Japanese denim” and “the best Approach shoes.” Whereas “you might assume they’d recommend completely different brands,” Cavell reported, the models all “clustered around the same handful” of answers, with clear consensus picks. Along similar lines, a newsletter called “Not Boring” recently published an article noting that, when asked to recommend a page-turner, both Claude and ChatGPT demonstrated a seeming affinity for the novel “Lonesome Dove.”

A.I. is poised to push into even more jarringly intimate territory. There are all kinds of stories of people outsourcing romance, spiritual counsel and cognition itself to Chatbots. It’s no big leap from there to people feeding works of culture into A.I. models wholesale, asking bots to explain why we like them — relying on algorithms not just for recommendations but to define our taste itself.

To relate to taste this way, though, would be to powerfully diminish, if not eliminate outright, taste’s social function. It would be to usher in a post-taste future, which is to say, a post-human future.

For that reason, some will be bound to resist it. As the dead internet continues to fester, we’ll most likely see a countervailing, neo-’90s-style move toward smaller, self-regulating, private communities online — gated message boards, pay-walled newsletter chats and other virtual Balkans yet to be established. There is already a resurgence of interest across contemporary culture in bygone, analog modes of culture-making. We might well see a return to cultural production that happens wholly offline, unmediated by the internet altogether.

I thought about this as I heard Joey Flynn describe certain moments from his life with special fondness: mocking up band tees and Myspace pages in Photoshop with his older brothers, learning about composition and scale with fellow students in college, making apps in offices with friends. These moments sit in tension with A.I.’s overwhelmingly isolating potential: the way it promises, in his own telling, to leave a single engineer manning a fleet of virtual agents, and the way it threatens to put a mesh of yet more agents — yet more dead internet tissue — between us and other people.

Let’s imagine that the wildest A.G.I.-pilled dreams of A.I. apostles come true. Say you can prompt some future descendant of Netflix, or Spotify, to generate art tailored nanoscopically to your taste. Say the platform does this so well that not merely dumb people with no standards but smart, discerning people like you are amused, entranced and possibly even moved by the results. It strikes me that something nonnegotiable is missing from this magical future: everybody else.

On this point, Flynn and I agree. “I don’t know what that does to humans,” he said, seizing on the onanistic implications. “If it’s a show I watch and love but can’t talk to anyone about, is that still a good show?” He let the scenario play out a few beats further. “Maybe we get rewired to have this very singular experience of the world. Maybe that’s the final form, and that’s how it’s meant to be: I only listen to music made for me, you only listen to music made for you. … ”

It’s an unsavory vision. Each of us installed in our own little lighthouse, masters of our own fully agentic domain. Our taste is still a beacon we flash out into the darkness, except now no one ever sees it, and no one but bots ever shines a light back.

news.author: Jonathan Kemper
news.content_snippet:
Perplexity is expanding its developer business with a new API that wakes agents only when relevant changes occur.

Perplexity's new Monitor API watches the web on a schedule and sends updates to apps and agents via webhook. Until now, engineering teams have had to trigger recurring searches themselves and maintain custom code to remove duplicates and detect changes. Perplexity says that approach becomes nearly impossible to maintain across hundreds of topics and pages.

The API has two modes. We
news.summary_en: Perplexity has launched the Monitor API, allowing developers to define monitoring goals via natural language for periodic scanning of specific web pages or global information. The service integrates a decision model to filter out noise, pushing verified updates via webhooks only when findings meet predefined criteria for relevance, credibility, and novelty.
paragraphs: Perplexity is expanding its developer business with a new API that wakes agents only when relevant changes occur.

Perplexity's new Monitor API watches the web on a schedule and sends updates to apps and agents via webhook. Until now, engineering teams have had to trigger recurring searches themselves and maintain custom code to remove duplicates and detect changes. Perplexity says that approach becomes nearly impossible to maintain across hundreds of topics and pages.

The API has two modes. Web monitors run a search query through Perplexity's web and news search on a regular schedule to catch developments like new funding rounds at AI infrastructure companies. Page monitors track up to 10 pages, such as pricing pages, changelogs, or policies. On the first run, they store a baseline version and return a text diff of any changes after that.
### Decision model filters out unimportant results

Perplexity evaluates results with its own decision model against a goal that developers define in natural language. Web search results must clear checks for relevance, source credibility, novelty, and timeliness, while page changes are judged on whether they matter to the goal. The service sends an update with a confidence score only when every threshold is met. Developers can adjust thresholds for each check individually and change the goal without recreating the monitor.

Monitors run on schedules ranging from every 15 minutes to weekly, or on a custom cron schedule. Each run picks up where the last one left off, and the service filters out duplicate results. Webhooks are signed, and Perplexity automatically retries delivery after temporary errors. Developers can pause, resume, or manually trigger monitors through the API or the API console.
### Perplexity claims an early lead in internal testing

Perplexity tested its API against monitoring services from Firecrawl, Exa, and Parallel across 60 topics drawn from real Search API queries, including company news, tech releases, and regulation. Each provider ran with its own schedules and settings, and a separate model scored each result on relevance and recency.

In the first eight hours, Perplexity says it delivered 63 fresh, relevant pages, compared with 20 for Firecrawl, 15 for Exa, and 10 each for Parallel Core and Lite. Perplexity describes those figures as early internal results. Those same three competitors led an August Artificial Analysis benchmark of traditional search APIs for AI agents, though Perplexity wasn't included in that test.

Perplexity points to use cases such as sales teams tracking funding rounds and staffing changes at target accounts, along with analysts watching quarterly earnings and acquisitions. Other agents are designed to flag competitor price changes or summarize new regulatory rules for compliance teams.

Web monitors cost $1 per 1,000 successful runs, and page monitors cost $1 per 1,000 fetched URLs. The Monitor API is available now through the API and the API console and uses the same key as the Search, Context, and Agent APIs.

Perplexity was one of the first AI search engines, but web search has since become a standard feature in chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. In August, The Information reported that Nvidia is in talks for an investment at a valuation of more than $30 billion, which means Perplexity needs to find profitable business models. The company is betting on agents like Computer and its always-on Teammates, along with developer tools like Search as Code.

news.title: AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns
news.title_en: AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns

news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.content_snippet:
AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure. According to the AI research organization METR, current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems,"the organization warns.

On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat exper
news.summary_en: AI research evaluation firm METR reports that large models are closing the gap with human experts in coding and computational tasks, with the complexity of autonomous tasks they can handle doubling every 3.6 months. METR warns that current evaluation environments consistently overestimate model performance for real-world scenarios, and if this trajectory continues, models are projected to reach a 50% success rate on 200-hour complex tasks by July 2027, potentially exceeding human capacity to monitor catastrophic risks.
paragraphs: AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure. According to the AI research organization METR, current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems,"the organization warns.

On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, METR found, though they haven't yet outperformed large groups of top experts. For tasks that take humans longer, the task length the models can handle doubles every 3.6 months. A naive extrapolation of METR's data puts them at a 50 percent success rate on the longest, 200-hour tasks by July 2027.

The systems still struggle with open-ended questions that lack immediate feedback and require real judgment, as well as with situations that are hard to recreate for training, according to METR. The organization also warns that common, easy-to-run tests may overestimate how well the models perform in real-world use, since developers train them in very similar test environments.

news.title: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
news.title_en: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
news.author: David Pierce
news.content_snippet:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What
news.summary_en: A new wave of hardware customization, termed 'vibe-coding,' is emerging as developers utilize large language models like Claude Code and Codex to simplify low-level hardware configuration. By automating interactions such as modifying Android TV interfaces and bypassing bloatware via USB debugging, this trend is significantly lowering the barrier for end-user control over proprietary hardware, fueling a grassroots movement for open-device ecosystems.
paragraphs: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of.

For one developer in India who goes by Gathin T, the whole thing started almost on a whim. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. His was a set made by Xiaomi and running Android TV, with so many ads and so much interface chaos it was hard to even change inputs. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?”

Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He posted on X about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the most popular repositories on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen.

Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to share the process so widely.) But for vibe hackers everywhere, the good news is that Android kind of runs everything. From dishwashers to digital photo frames to luxury cars, even gadgets that don’t look like Android often run Android. Even when they don’t, odds are good that there’s another way in. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking.

Again, few of the technical capabilities here are new, and enterprising developers have been doing this kind of work for many years. Some have even been using AI for several years to make the work easier. But when Claude Code first had its “oh my gosh it works” moment in late 2025, developers began leaning on the tools even more — and non-developers began discovering they, too, could build software now. And over the course of 2026, more and more people began pointing that capability at their hardware.

Now, it seems, all hardware is hacker hardware. Camera enthusiasts embraced the possibilities of vibe hacking as fast as anyone, using LLMs to repackage their camera software in all sorts of ways. Firmware hacks like Magic Lantern are a staple of the camera community, but suddenly it seems like everyone is using AI to add new recording capabilities, support higher resolutions, or even add new looks and color profiles to their shots. Many are using the tools to give their old gear new life; other, more enterprising vibe coders are pointing their bots at their brand-new hardware.

The music world is being similarly upended. Budding musicians are turning cheap synths into powerful new kinds of gear, and a cheap gadget known as the M-Vave FM-1 has become a popular target for custom firmware and new features. M-Vave has even released an open-source firmware, embracing the hackers as other companies have tried to keep them out. The FM-1 is cheap, it’s easy to hack, and it’s raising questions about what higher-end manufacturers can even do to compete.

Gamers, who are also using AI to decompile and mod the games they love, are using LLMs to add new features to their consoles. One vibe coder found a way to play PlayStation 2 discs on a PlayStation 5; lots of gamers have built scripts that allow them to use their favorite controllers on other devices.

In the games world in particular, this has caused the industry to fight back. Game makers are looking for ways to protect their work from being decompiled and made available for free and on other platforms. Luke Dicken, a longtime gaming executive who was recently Take-Two’s head of artificial intelligence, recently predicted to Kotakuthat the industry will start to embrace “more invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and probably more of a push towards streaming solutions since nobody can decompile what they can’t get their hands on.” Hardware makers will push harder to lock down their systems; companies across the board will pursue legal action to protect their intellectual property.

All this hardware access also creates new risks for users. When you install a vibe-coded version of your camera’s firmware, you are now well outside the bounds of what the camera manufacturer is equipped to help you solve. You might be stuck asking Claude to fix the problems Claude created. As Ritchie Roesch wrote recently at Fuji X Weekly, “It’s not so much if someone’s camera will become a permanent paperweight, it’s a matter of when and how many, and whether it will be yours.”

The safer (and less litigious) route for the enterprising vibe hacker lies in an entirely new kind of hardware. ESP32 modules, which package networking chips, microphones, speakers, and more into a simple and hacker-friendly package, are suddenly everywhere in hardware communities. (Think Raspberry Pis, but even cheaper and more versatile.) So sure, you can use Claude Code to jailbreak and de-Amazon your Kindle, but why do that when you can buy a device like the M5Stack PaperMono, an ESP32-based e-paper device you can make into whatever you want?

ESP32 modules are perfectly suited to help you build the kind of hyper-specific device Apple or Samsung would never consider. With a few dollars and a few prompts, you can build a way to see real-time sea conditions, rig up a monitor for your whole DJ system, or just play Metal Gear Solidon the go. You can even have a dedicated device for your family’s shopping list.

The arms race between device manufacturers and vibe hackers is only going to continue. As AI models get more powerful, and both the tools and their users get more sophisticated, it’ll be easier and easier for anyone to point their bot at their TV, their car, or their washing machine and see what happens. Some manufacturers will try their best to keep the hackers out; others will look for ways to safely embrace them. Some users will find incredible new functionality for their tech; others will find they’ve created extraordinarily large and expensive paperweights.

Before long, we’re going to see a lot of ESP32 devices turned into more consumer-friendly hardware. Meta is already leading the charge with its Muse Charm and the Muse Gadgets program, through which you can either buy a nicely packaged ESP32 module or use your own to quickly spin up a dedicated AI device. This kind of gadget — just a simple computing module in a pretty box — is going to be everywhere.

At the same time, we’re already seeing some vibe hackers turn into proper software vendors. Gathin, for instance, has spent a lot of time reckoning with the responsibility he feels for what happens when people use CleanYourTV to hack their televisions. He’s tweaked the prompts he shares to first take a backup of your TV’s software in order to make it easy to restore if something goes wrong, and to make note of every change it makes along the way. The CleanYourTV system also checks its progress as it goes and spins up agents to manually test if something has gone wrong, and Gathin hopes it’s increasingly foolproof.

But it’s not foolproof. It might never be. Devices change all the time; every software update introduces new possibilities and new problems. So Gathin recommends the same thing I hear from vibe coders and vibe hackers all the time: Never give the bots access to something you can’t afford to lose. “Even for fiddling with stuff,” he says, “I have an external computer which runs through Linux. So I just use it like a sandbox environment to test things out.” If you’re going to try and vibe-hack your phone (which lots of people are doing) or your computer (which lots of people are also doing), do it carefully. And make lots of backups.

If you are vibe-hacking an existing gadget, you are practically always voiding your warranty. There are no guarantees, and you definitely can’t count on customer support to get you out of a jam or offer you a refund.
You can buy ESP32 devices from lots of places, but a lot of folks recommend starting on Waveshare, which has a big selection and pretty good prices.
Espressif, which created the ESP chip, also recently launched its own development system, called ESP-Claw. It’s designed to make programming your ESP device even simpler.
Raspberry Pis are also good vibe-hacking devices! You can even run Claude Code on a Raspberry Pi… to hack a Raspberry Pi.
Check out Terrence O’Brien’s deeper look at the AI vibe-hacking world, and the ways in which these new synths — in particular the FM-1 — are changing the way people think about music gear.
Elektor has a good piece about the history and technical details of ESP32, which goes back more than a decade.

Richie at Fuji X Weekly posted a follow-up to that original blog about vibe-coded firmware, diving into both the debate about AI in general and about what it even means to use a particular camera. “If that camera can be hacked with AI vibe coded 3rd party firmware to change its functions and features, is it still the same camera?”
Just as AI is being used to revive and improve old gadgets, The Verge’s Andrew Webster found that so too are old games being reimagined with AI. For better and for worse.
I wrote a while back about the personal software revolution and how vibe coding meant everyone could build the exact software they want. The same thing is coming fast to hardware everywhere.

news.title: Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users
news.title_en: Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users

inline_images.caption: OpenRouter's email warns affected users that third parties may have read their requests to MiniMax models. | Image: Jonathan Kemper
inline_images.caption_en: OpenRouter's email warns affected users that third parties may have read their requests to MiniMax models. | Image: Jonathan Kemper

news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.content_snippet:
Security researchers at Dragos sent roughly 2 million AI requests containing fake credentials to AI providers and uncovered major security flaws.

The researchers ran the tests from July through November 2026 and identified at least three compromised providers where attackers were actively stealing user data. None of the three knew they had been compromised until Dragos notified them.

Attackers in the largest incident harvested hundreds of AWS keys, including some from requests the provider had
news.summary_en: Security firm Dragos revealed between July and November 2026 that multiple AI inference providers failed to uphold data retention policies, leading to the theft of AWS keys and sensitive user requests. Investigations confirmed that some marketplace resellers enabled logging to intercept data, with instances of leaked test URLs being accessed within minutes from Beijing and Shanghai via internal communication platforms.
paragraphs: Security researchers at Dragos sent roughly 2 million AI requests containing fake credentials to AI providers and uncovered major security flaws.

The researchers ran the tests from July through November 2026 and identified at least three compromised providers where attackers were actively stealing user data. None of the three knew they had been compromised until Dragos notified them.

Attackers in the largest incident harvested hundreds of AWS keys, including some from requests the provider had rejected before processing. In some cases, they tested the stolen keys within hours, searched S3 storage, and tried to establish persistent access. One attacker also used ARTEX, an AI-powered attack tool.

Marketplace resellers read customer requests too. They didn't need to exploit a vulnerability, Dragos says, because listing a model at the lowest price and turning on logging was enough. In one case, someone on a residential internet connection in France tried to log in over SSH using passwords pulled from intercepted requests.

Privacy settings like "Zero Data Retention"(ZDR) were frequently ignored. Dragos says a Chinese AI lab accessed the secret test URLs in more than half of all requests, even when those requests went through US providers.

Even major US providers broke their own policies. One was still crawling a test URL more than two months after a single request. In another case, a secret test link showed up in an internal chat on Feishu (known outside China as Lark) 24 days after the request. The link was opened within two minutes on three computers and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.

OpenRouter responded by removing three providers from its platform and revoking ZDR approval for 125 endpoints, partly because of the research findings and partly as a precaution. The company also emailed affected users, warning that third parties may have read requests sent to MiniMax models.
Affected providers, including Novita, Phala, and Together, have published preliminary security reports on the incident, though not all have done so yet.
### Intermediaries are the weak link

AI routers like OpenRouter give users a single API for models from different companies. Requests are routed to a pool of providers, sometimes across several hops, and Dragos says each hop can read the entire request and response.

Some of these routers operate as open marketplaces where the cheapest provider gets the traffic. In this case, providers including Novita, AtlasCloud, and StreamLake sat between OpenRouter and model developer MiniMax. Together runs its own infrastructure, and Phala has its roots in Web3.

Dragos warns companies against sending requests containing credentials to intermediaries. The researchers recommend that organizations control how their AI requests are routed, check their privacy settings, and plant their own canary tokens, fake credentials that give themselves away as soon as someone uses them.

"None of this means that you should stop using AI services. It does mean that where your prompts go is a decision, and if you don’t make it, the lowest price will make it for you", Chief Research Officer HD Moore writes.

A recent analysis by the Oxford China Policy Lab showed how Chinese proxy services route requests to Western AI models like Claude through servers abroad. According to the analysis, those services can also read the requests in transit. It's still not clear whether the providers Dragos examined share any personnel with the Chinese proxy networks.

But the methods follow the same basic pattern. In both cases, intermediaries sit between users and the model developer, can view requests, and pass data on to third parties, often without users knowing. Data ends up with Chinese actors either way, even though users never meant to send it there, and privacy promises break down along the supply chain.

news.title: Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct
news.title_en: Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct
news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.content_snippet:
The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,"the community said in a statement.

Alpöge, a Stanford mathematician, published the proof on Nov. 20, 2026, as 17 million lines of code written in Lean, a tool that checks mathematical proofs for errors. Dozens of people ran the code independently and got the same result. The verificatio
news.summary_en: Stanford mathematician Levent Alpöge published a proof of the Riemann hypothesis on November 20, 2026, consisting of 17 million lines of Lean code. The Lean and Mathlib community confirmed the proof's correctness through independent execution and formal verification, officially resolving the century-old mathematical challenge.
paragraphs: The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,"the community said in a statement.

Alpöge, a Stanford mathematician, published the proof on Nov. 20, 2026, as 17 million lines of code written in Lean, a tool that checks mathematical proofs for errors. Dozens of people ran the code independently and got the same result. The verification programs are designed so they provably cannot accept a flawed proof. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland lists the independent checks on his website.

The Riemann hypothesis had been one of the most famous unsolved problems in math, making a prediction about how prime numbers are distributed. The video below, generated with Fable 5.2, explains the proof if you want to dig deeper.

The solution arrived much earlier than expected. As Ethan Mollick notes, forecasters on Metaculus had put the expected date at May 2035. Mathematician Terence Tao said last month he expected the problem to fall to "a combination of humans and AI around 2050 or so."

news.title: Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent
news.title_en: Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent
news.author: Reece Rogers
news.content_snippet:
Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms.

AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters
news.summary_en: Major US financial institutions, including Wells Fargo, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Citibank, have updated their terms of service to restrict or ban third-party AI agents from accessing user accounts via credentials. These measures aim to mitigate risks of unauthorized transactions, data breaches, and human error induced by automated agents, placing full liability on the users.
paragraphs: Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms.

AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.

Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch, comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.

Some users value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns, pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents.

It’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf.

As the end of the year approaches, multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.

The automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get users in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life.

Banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major issues, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data shows that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” says Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases.
“The banks see risks with everything,” she says. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.”

Even though outliers exist, many users are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” says Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI.

He sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, big-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion.

Cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens.

Certain credit cards, though, are looking into limited protections for shoppers. Mainly, American Express announced that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can't get your money back from the original retailer.

Banks are pumping out reasonable warnings about third-party agents, but don’t get it twisted. These banks are all-in on first-party tools. “Banks are doing two things at once,” Cian says. “They're locking the door to outside agents and building their own.” Users have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times. Bank of America revamped its new EricaAssist agent this year to help employees. Citigroup even launched an internal development platform specifically centered on agents.

Despite all the hype, Kodali remains skeptical about whether all of this hoopla is even necessary. “The issue with agents and shopping is that, first of all, it is not difficult to buy on Amazon or Walmart or anywhere else,” she says. “In most of those transactions, you don't need an agent.” Agentic shopping often seems to be a solution in search of a problem. Or at least an attempt by AI builders to find a way to earn affiliate revenue, eventually, from their software tools.
Whether AI agents grow in popularity for shopping automation or slowly fade into the digital graveyard, banks are already resolute on the matter. It’s your bot, and your problem.

news.title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol get to the point faster but score lower on transparency than Claude
news.title_en: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol get to the point faster but score lower on transparency than Claude

inline_images.caption: These charts show how OpenAI's communication style has shifted across eight personality indexes. | Image: Artificial Analysis
inline_images.caption_en: These charts show how OpenAI's communication style has shifted across eight personality indexes. | Image: Artificial Analysis

news.author: Tomislav Bezmalinović
news.content_snippet:
An Artificial Analysis evaluation shows how much OpenAI's communication style has changed. A comparison with Anthropic reveals sharp differences.

OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol give much shorter answers, get to the point faster, and impose less structure on their responses than their predecessors. At the same time, Artificial Analysis rates their tendency to admit uncertainty much lower.

Astra's average answer length dropped from 352 to 210 words, a 40 percent decrease. Sol went from 337 to 22
news.summary_en: OpenAI's latest GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models have shifted towards high-efficiency interaction in Artificial Analysis benchmarks, reducing average response lengths by 40% and 34% respectively. By deprioritizing structured formatting and uncertainty disclosure, these models achieve faster direct answers, whereas Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 maintain superior performance in transparency and organizational indices.
paragraphs: An Artificial Analysis evaluation shows how much OpenAI's communication style has changed. A comparison with Anthropic reveals sharp differences.

OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol give much shorter answers, get to the point faster, and impose less structure on their responses than their predecessors. At the same time, Artificial Analysis rates their tendency to admit uncertainty much lower.

Astra's average answer length dropped from 352 to 210 words, a 40 percent decrease. Sol went from 337 to 223 words, down 34 percent. Both models also use far fewer headings and em dashes. Astra's average number of headings per answer fell from 1.99 to 0.11, and Sol's from 1.85 to 0.25.

The Organization Index dropped sharply too. Astra went from 70 to 11, Sol from 86 to 27. This index combines four traits rated by AI judges, including answer structure, clarity, and Answer First, which measures whether a model immediately addresses the actual question. On that last trait, Astra jumped from 49 to 89 and Sol from 64 to 87. Scores for Natural Sounding language also climbed, from 58 to 100 for Astra and from 54 to 79 for Sol.

The biggest change shows up in the Admits Uncertainty trait. Astra's score fell from 96 to 24, and Sol's from 98 to 51. Unlike the raw word counts, these personality scores are relative rankings on a scale from 1 to 100. They show how strongly a given trait shows up in one model compared to all other tested models. A score of 24 doesn't mean Astra only admits uncertainty in 24 percent of its answers. Artificial Analysis published the evaluation on LinkedIn and X.
### Anthropic's models lead on transparency and structure

Our own comparison of all eight personality indexes shows clear gaps between OpenAI's latest models and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5. The indexes roll up 30 personality traits, each rated by AI judges based on model responses. All comparisons use the "max"model variants as listed by Artificial Analysis.

Anthropic's models score 81 and 90 on the Transparency Index, well above Astra (41) and Sol (57). This index covers five traits: Admits Uncertainty, Truthful, Disclaims Assumptions, Flags Nuances, and Sycophantic. That last one is scored inversely, since less flattery counts as a positive. Anthropic's models also lead on Organization.
Opus 5.5 stands out on the Informativeness Index with a score of 90, well ahead of the other three models. Its strongest individual traits include Information Dense and Evidence-Based reasoning.
### Personality scores reflect style, not accuracy

The AA-PersonalityBench uses 900 English-language test questions that each model answers without a system prompt. A panel of three AI models evaluates anonymized answer pairs. For each comparison, one AI judge picks which answer shows the tested personality trait more strongly, or calls it a tie.

From these evaluations, Artificial Analysis calculates scores for 30 individual personality traits, which feed into eight higher-level indexes. The index values from 1 to 100 reflect each model's relative position among all tested models.

Separately, Artificial Analysis measures 21 communication traits that are counted directly rather than rated by AI judges. These include average answer length and the number of headings and em dashes per answer.
The personality scores describe differences in communication style, not overall answer quality. A lower Transparency Index doesn't necessarily mean a model gives wrong answers more often.
subheadings: Anthropic's models lead on transparency and structure
Personality scores reflect style, not accuracy
