news.title: China’s Spies Set Sights on A.I. Chips Years Before Nvidia Scandal
news.title_en: China’s Spies Set Sights on A.I. Chips Years Before Nvidia Scandal

inline_images.caption: Chen Yixin, now the head of China’s spy agency, in 2018, when he was a party leader in Wuhan. (Agence France-Presse — Getty Images)
inline_images.alt: Chen Yixin, now the head of China’s spy agency, in 2018, when he was a party leader in Wuhan.

inline_images.caption: Nvidia’s Blackwell and Rubin chips, as depicted in a presentation that Jensen Huang made in March. (Manuel Orbegozo for The New York Times)
inline_images.alt: Nvidia’s Blackwell and Rubin chips, as depicted in a presentation that Jensen Huang made in March.

inline_images.caption: Jensen Huang and Alice Huang in Taipei in June 2024. (Ann Wang/Reuters)
inline_images.alt: Jensen Huang and Alice Huang in Taipei in June 2024.

news.author: Chris Buckley and Julian E. Barnes
news.content_snippet:
When China’s top espionage agency updated its priorities this year, it added a revealing goal: overcoming Western barriers to technologies that Xi Jinping sees as crucial to China’s rise.

At the heart of that quest are the advanced semiconductors needed to power artificial intelligence, including chips that the United States has barred U.S. companies like Nvidia from exporting to China.

China must “adopt extraordinary measures to intensify the drive for core technologies in priority sectors,”
news.summary_en: China's Ministry of State Security, led by Minister Chen Yixin, has established a specialized task force reporting directly to him to bypass U.S. semiconductor export restrictions. The unit focuses on illicit procurement of restricted high-end Nvidia AI chips and intelligence gathering on key chip executives to counter Western technological blockades.
paragraphs: When China’s top espionage agency updated its priorities this year, it added a revealing goal: overcoming Western barriers to technologies that Xi Jinping sees as crucial to China’s rise.

At the heart of that quest are the advanced semiconductors needed to power artificial intelligence, including chips that the United States has barred U.S. companies like Nvidia from exporting to China.

China must “adopt extraordinary measures to intensify the drive for core technologies in priority sectors,” Mr. Xi told the Politburo, a council of senior officials, in January, according to an official text of his speech. “As swiftly as possible, solve the ‘chokehold’ problems holding back development of future industries.”

The spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, has long been dedicated to eliminating threats to Communist Party rule in China. Now, it has made it a priority to acquire advanced semiconductor chips and gather intelligence about them, according to several serving and former security and intelligence officials from governments outside China in Asia, the United States and Europe.

How China’s spy agency is seeking to obtain advanced chips and intelligence about them has become a central question in the case of Alice Huang. She is a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. officials say the Chinese agency was working with to spy on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the American chip giant Nvidia, allegations that were first reported by The New York Times.
Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment and China has rejected the claims of espionage as “pure fabrication.”

The Chinese spy agency’s campaign to acquire chips, details of which have not been previously reported, has been underway for at least two years, according to the current and former officials. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence.
Among the campaign’s main elements:

The head of the spy agency, Chen Yixin, who holds the title of minister of state security, created a working team that is leading the effort and reports directly to him, multiple foreign officials said. Mr. Chen has worked under Mr. Xi since they were officials in Zhejiang Province in eastern China, a cradle of China’s high-tech boom.
The group was assigned to help China’s “counter-blockade” work — efforts to overcome export controls imposed by the United States and its allies.
The campaign includes helping Chinese companies acquire and smuggle advanced chips into China.
The group also collects intelligence about the semiconductor sector and its supply chains, according to several officials briefed on the campaign.

In April, Mr. Chen unveiled the new mission. “Deepen the struggle against blockades, and comprehensively advance artificial intelligence innovation, industry development, and applications,” Mr. Chen wrote in a Communist Party journal.
“Focus on tackling the ‘chokeholds’ of critical technologies,” he wrote, and solve the problem of technologies that “cannot be obtained by asking, buying or pleading.”

“Chen is signaling to the party leadership and his own ranks that his agency is elevating A.I. competition with the U.S. as a long-term, top priority,” said Alex Joske, the managing director of security practice at Garnaut Global, a consultancy firm, who studies the Chinese security apparatus. “He is telling his officers to find more ways to wage this struggle.”

The ministry’s campaign is part of a wider push by the ruling Communist Party to overcome Western-imposed restrictions on critical technology. China is determined to close its gap with the United States in the computing capacity needed for progress in artificial intelligence.

At the top, that effort is being coordinated by the Central Science and Technology Commission. The commission is a secretive Communist Party organ that Mr. Xi established in 2023. This was not long after the U.S. Commerce Department, in late 2022, started banning exports of Nvidia’s advanced chips directly to China, out of concern the chips could help Beijing crack American encryption and design new weapons.
The party commission is ranked higher than ministries and is led by Ding Xuexiang, one of only seven members of the Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee, its inner circle of power.

“Computing power is a major indicator of overall national power,” Mr. Ding said in May when he visited energy and computing facilities in Beijing and nearby regions that are part of a planned nationwide A.I. computing network, according to Xinhua, China’s official news agency.
Mr. Xi created the commission to better marshal the country’s scientists, institutes and labs across ministries, and companies, for national priorities such as achieving technological self-reliance.

The Commission rarely surfaces in Chinese news reports; its budgets and plans are not made public. But it has become an engine of Mr. Xi’s plans for technological pre-eminence, said Christopher K. Johnson, a former Central Intelligence Agency analyst focused on China. The director of the commission, Mr. Ding, has long been a close aide to Mr. Xi and is also a vice premier overseeing science and technology policy.

China’s espionage service and other parts of the government have for decades pursued technology and research from abroad, using both open and illicit methods. But under Mr. Xi, that effort assumed greater urgency, with more top-level coordination, including in artificial intelligence, several experts said.
Throughout this year, Mr. Chen, the agency’s chief, has repeatedly said the “anti-blockade struggle” is one of the key duties of China’s Ministry of State Security.

“Certain countries are going to every length to impose a ‘chokehold’ on China in fields of critical technology,” Mr. Chen wrote in a party journal last year. “Technology competition among the major powers has entered its most intense, most strenuous and most critical phase of close-quarters combat.”

As American companies, followed by Chinese ones, developed successively powerful A.I. models, officials in Beijing have increasingly recognized the potential for artificial intelligence to threaten their power at home and abroad, said Gregory C. Allen, the founder and chief executive of Decision Tree Research, a firm that specializes in A.I. and other advanced technologies.

In September, Mr. Chen himself referred to U.S. tech companies and their A.I. models — like Claude Mythos and GPT-5.5-Cyber — as examples of new cybersecurity threats, as he described the risks that A.I. posed to the party’s hold on power.

“China’s senior leadership understands that A.I. is critically, strategically essential, and that leadership in A.I. is obviously related to leadership in semiconductors,” said Mr. Allen, a former senior official at the U.S. Department of Defense’s Joint Artificial Intelligence Center.

Mr. Chen became the state security minister in late 2022, and just over a year later the ministry issued a warning that A.I. was “highly likely in the near future to profoundly transform the national security landscape.” In 2024, the ministry said that its officers were scoring successes against the attempts of “the United States and other Western countries to lock us in at the low-end” of technology.
China has sometimes used front organizations or researchers to collect information about foreign A.I. technology, said Mr. Joske, the consultant.
“M.S.S. is very comfortable using business covers,” he said, “and it’s very comfortable running people as assets without directly telling those people that they’re working for the M.S.S.”

Such covers could include organizations ostensibly focused on academic research. In September, MI5, the British security agency, asserted that a Chinese research institute linked to the Chinese spy agency had drawn in British scientists for research that, apparently unbeknown to the scientists, “directly improves M.S.S. technical capability for espionage.”
Companies such as the one Alice Huang founded, Megaspeed, are viewed as another potential vehicle for gathering intelligence.

The precise nature of Alice Huang’s role in the ministry’s chip effort remains unclear. U.S. officials say Ms. Huang, who was having an affair with the Nvidia founder Mr. Huang, passed information to Beijing about him. The U.S. government is also investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling advanced chips into China.

Megaspeed, which is based in Singapore, bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and entered the business of providing high-end computing capacity to Chinese companies. Such services have allowed Chinese businesses to use Nvidia chips at data centers abroad by sidestepping U.S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A.I. chips directly to Chinese firms.

Last week, The Times also reported that Megaspeed was possibly aiding a lab with links to China’s military, through Alibaba, the Chinese internet giant. Alibaba is a customer and financial backer of Megaspeed. Providing Nvidia chips to support research for China’s military would be a violation of U.S. law.

An Alibaba spokeswoman said: “Any suggestions that Alibaba provides services to the military is groundless. Alibaba Cloud’s service agreement strictly prohibits the use of our products and services for any military purpose.”

In an effort to address what many in Washington see as a loophole, the Trump administration announced on Monday that it would move ahead with a new rule to prevent China from being able to access advanced semiconductors from Nvidia and other U.S. companies through the use of data centers outside China.

The new restriction will require overseas data centers to obtain a government license before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in countries on a list that includes China, Russia and Iran. It goes into effect in about 90 days.
The restriction could make China’s pursuit of self-reliance more urgent, a goal Mr. Xi has cast as a fight for survival, echoing the party’s revolutionary past.

“Like the Red Army on the Long March, we’re now on a new Long March,” he told technicians, while visiting an A.I. data hub under construction in northern China last month. He was referring to a grueling trek taken by Communist troops in the 1930s that cemented Mao’s leadership of the revolution. “You are an army in the drive for advanced technological self-reliance.”

The Role of Businesses and Other Groups

news.author: Nikou Asgari
news.content_snippet: Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro demand more for equipment, with the increased costs hitting trading firms
news.summary_en: Global data center equipment suppliers are significantly increasing prices for previously contracted AI servers, with hikes reaching up to 45%. This surge is driven by extreme supply-demand imbalances in AI infrastructure, forcing manufacturers to bypass existing contract terms to pass on rising memory and component costs.
news.title_zh: AI服务器供应吃紧，供应商违约提价达45%

fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】数据中心设备供应商；Nvidia系AI服务器买方在全球数据中心硬件供应链：在合同签订后强行将AI服务器售价上调至多45%

【关键数据与实测】合同签订后执行45%的提价，供应链议价逻辑发生剧变。
【行业影响与走向】市场影响：算力采购从财务预算驱动转向紧迫的供应保障驱动。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Data center equipment suppliers; Buyers of Nvidia-powered AI servers: Unilaterally increasing AI server prices by up to 45% post-contract
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Explosive demand for AI compute infrastructure and upstream memory shortages squeezing supplier margins
[Key Metrics] 45% price hike post-contract, shift in supply chain bargaining power.
[Industry Impact & Outlook] Market impact: Transition from budget-driven to supply-security-driven compute procurement.
paragraphs: Tech companies that sell equipment for data centres are significantly raising prices for Nvidia-powered AI servers, months after contracts with buyers have been signed, as soaring AI infrastructure prices are passed down to customers.

Suppliers including Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro sell servers containing components such as graphics processing units — the primary AI processors made by the likes of Nvidia and AMD — as well as memory chips and networking gear to customers who are building their own data centres. Such deals are typically agreed well in advance of delivery.

Months later, when the equipment is ready to be delivered, these tech companies are demanding substantially higher prices than the figures originally agreed, according to people familiar with the matter.

Even large financial services and trading firms, which are among the biggest buyers of computing equipment after the Big Tech hyperscalers, are at the mercy of their suppliers’ pricing power, at a time when demand for AI equipment is far outstripping supply.

The price rises are hitting some of the world’s biggest financial trading firms, including Jane Street, Optiver and Hudson River Trading, as they build vast data centres to power the research that underpins their trading, the people said.

“It is disconcerting when you get a 25, 30, 45 per cent [price increase],” said one person familiar with the matter. “There is a significant disparity” between the price initially agreed months in advance and the amount that companies end up paying once the components are delivered, they added.

The price jumps highlight the ferocious demand for computing power, as tech giants, trading firms and other large companies race to create their own data centres. The price rises are largely due to tech companies passing on soaring memory costs, which have risen more than 400 per cent since the start of 2024, according to JPMorgan research.
“The standard now is we’ll sign a contract with an indicative price and the price could be arbitrarily high by the time they deliver it,” said another person familiar with the matter.
“We’ve never said no,” they added. “At the end of the day, the compute is valuable to us and we’ll pay for it.”
Buyers approached by the FT did not confirm whether the contracts included terms stating that prices might increase by the time of order delivery.
Financial trading firms are huge buyers of AI equipment and are largely agreeing to the higher costs because they need the specialised equipment to build their data centres.

Trading companies are building vast data centres around the world to fuel the research that underpins their secretive and highly profitable trading strategies. Hudson River Trading runs a big data centre in a converted underground mine in Norway, while British firm XTX Markets is building its own data centres in Finland.
HPE and Supermicro declined to comment. Dell and Lenovo did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Hudson River Trading and Optiver declined to comment. Jane Street did not respond to requests for comment.
The price of GPU servers has risen at least 20 to 30 per cent, according to one of the people. CPU nodes, where memory is a large fraction of the cost, have tripled or more in price, they added.
One dispute over price rises was thrust into the open earlier this year, when it reached court.

In June, XTX sued Dell in Irish court. The companies had agreed a fixed price of $549mn for servers, plus XTX paid an extra $5mn to “ensure price certainty”. But Dell later told the British trading firm that component prices for the servers had increased and said XTX would have to pay “at least an additional $62-70mn to obtain the servers”, according to court filings.

“XTX was shocked that Dell sought to increase the agreed price,” the company said in court filings, which also claimed that Dell told XTX executives that “other companies faced with price increases had gone and looked at other suppliers but had come back to Dell and agreed to price adjustment increases”.
Dell told XTX that it “was not able to absorb those increased costs” from rising memory prices, XTX said in the court filing.
XTX declined to comment. Dell did not respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit. The case is ongoing.

paragraphs: SINGAPORE—Jensen Huang’s romantic partner was the public face of a business suspected of funneling advanced computing power to China. But playing a key role behind the scenes, according to people familiar with the matter, was a man now out on bail in Singapore, living in a luxury villa down the street from the Chinese embassy.

His name is Li Ming. The 52-year-old Chinese national was a central operator of a web of companies smuggling restricted Nvidia artificial-intelligence chips to China, the people said. This web included Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company where Huang’s paramour, Alice Huang, was a managing director. Li was deeply involved in Megaspeed’s activities and took part in major decisions, the people said, as well as playing a role in other companies trading Nvidia chips.

news.author: Terrence O'Brien
news.content_snippet:
One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.

The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely d
news.summary_en: UN diplomats failed to establish a legally binding framework for lethal autonomous weapons systems at the Geneva meeting, settling only on a two-year window to discuss potential regulatory options. Led by Russia, Israel, and the United States, significant resistance has stalled progress on defining enforceable compliance standards.
paragraphs: One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.

The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”

Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.
According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions:

news.author: Zijing Wu
news.content_snippet:
The Chinese businesswoman romantically linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had connections to a network for supplying AI chips that included an alleged Cambodian criminal enterprise, an FT investigation has found.

Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang is at the centre of US investigations into whether Nvidia’s largest client in south-east Asia was involved in the underground chip trade. Some US officials suspect Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, a claim Beijing dismissed as a “smear”.

Linke
news.summary_en: Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang is accused of orchestrating a complex shell company network to illicitly transfer advanced Nvidia AI chips to China. The network engaged cloud providers, gambling entities, and Cambodian organizations, utilizing infrastructure linked to former Nvidia partner Inspur to bypass US export controls.
paragraphs: The Chinese businesswoman romantically linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had connections to a network for supplying AI chips that included an alleged Cambodian criminal enterprise, an FT investigation has found.

Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang is at the centre of US investigations into whether Nvidia’s largest client in south-east Asia was involved in the underground chip trade. Some US officials suspect Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, a claim Beijing dismissed as a “smear”.

Linked to Alice Huang was a sprawling web of companies between Nvidia and China-based users of its chips that included cloud computing partners, online gaming tycoons, Cambodian traffickers and hundreds of shell companies, the FT found.

These seemingly unconnected enterprises combined — without necessarily being aware of the full picture — to make billions of dollars from one of the most profitable illicit trades in the world: moving Nvidia chips into China.

The FT traced the connections after speaking to more than a dozen people with knowledge of the operations, revealing links that were obscured by complex structures through hundreds of corporate filings.
Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial in developing cutting-edge AI and have become a vital commodity in the geopolitical rivalry between the US and China.

Washington’s export controls to prevent Beijing from acquiring the most powerful processors have created a multibillion-dollar black market to circumvent US curbs and satisfy China’s insatiable demand.

“Chip smuggling isn’t different from drugs or arms in terms of the structure of the supply chain. But there’s this importance attached to the semiconductor industry — it’s how the US wants to delay China in the AI race,” said Chris Clague, an associate fellow at International Institute for Strategic Studies who has focused on illicit trades in the past decade.

Moving advanced chips into China requires three main corporate channels: a group that is permitted to acquire and distribute the semiconductors; customers that do not fall foul of US export restrictions; and an underground network to smuggle the goods into China and money out.
The network linked to Alice Huang reached the US through Inspur, which was one of Nvidia’s largest partners for assembling chips into ready-to-use servers in China.

In March of 2023, Inspur was added to the US “entity list” for allegedly assisting the Chinese military. Some of its affiliates were also added to the register — but not Inspur’s part-owned US subsidiary, based in San Jose, California.
Inspur renamed the US unit Aivres, and since it was not on the entity list, it was able to keep trading with Nvidia.

Inside the chipmaker, there were questions about whether Aivres should qualify as an original equipment manufacturing (OEM) partner because of its links to Inspur, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. But Nvidia concluded the company met all compliance and export control requirements.

The second plank of the network was a customer that met the requirements to buy Nvidia chips at scale. OEM partners such as Aivres, which are allowed to integrate Nvidia GPUs into systems and sell those on, still needed to prove that their customers are not Chinese to access the US chipmaker’s products.
To be a qualified end customer, Nvidia requires at least three years of corporate records and proof that its management and owners are not majority Chinese.

Seeking to regain access to chip supplies, some of Inspur’s Chinese clients sought help from a successful online gaming company, Century Huatong, according to multiple people with knowledge of the matter.
Over two decades, the Chinese group had morphed from a car parts business into a gaming platform, finally emerging as a data centre investor with deep connections in the industry.

Century Huatong veterans discussed ways to gain access to the chips with its associates and business partners. The solution that emerged involved using an offshore shell company that would not trigger US export restrictions and could be branded as a “neocloud” provider.
That shell became Megaspeed, while Alice Huang fulfilled the requirement for a “trusted” outward-facing executive with a spotless record, according to people with knowledge of the arrangement.

Huang’s husband, Kang Wei, was an early investor in Century Huatong, according to Chinese corporate filings. His fund Hexi Investment also backed a 2020 Century Huatong data centre project with 7Road, a Shenzhen-based gaming company in which both Huang and Century Huatong had invested.
Alice Huang and Kang Wei did not respond to requests for comment.

7Road International, the offshore arm of 7Road, was the forerunner of Megaspeed, having had several years of clean corporate records in Singapore. In 2023, Huang acquired its unit in the city-state and renamed it.

An Nvidia spokesperson said: “We placed Megaspeed and a subsidiary on our block list in 2025 . . . we do not sell to them, and if one of our OEM customers identifies the company for any planned shipment, we do not approve the OEM sale.” Nvidia added that it had also restricted sales to Aivres.
Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment but has previously said that it “conducts legitimate and lawful business”.

With her English skills, Hong Kong residency and reputation as a good networker and dealmaker, Huang was seen as an ideal western-friendly representative, according to people who knew her at the time.
It also helped that she and her husband were already looking to move into data centre businesses in south-east Asia that would lease chips to Chinese tech companies.
“Alice was chosen [to lead Megaspeed] because of the trust built over years,” said a person who had business dealings with her around the time.
The third — and essential — element of the enterprise was finding a partner to move chips into China.

People familiar with the matter said that Hu Xiaowei, who US authorities say is a leading figure in a Cambodia-based syndicate sanctioned for cyber scams and money laundering, filled at least part of this role.

Hu, who was arrested in Japan in the summer, could not be reached for comment. He has been accused by US authorities of running smuggling and gambling rings as the “second-in-command” at Prince Group.
A spokesperson for the Prince group of companies said Hu has never worked for the business and there was “no evidence of the US government’s unsupported allegations”.
Hu made money from online gaming-related businesses that brought him into contact with Century Huatong, according to people with knowledge of the matter.
The connections between Hu and Century Huatong run through a complex web of shareholdings and an IP partnership spanning dozens of company records examined by the FT.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

One clear link can be traced through Wang Ji, Century Huatong’s chair and largest individual shareholder, who was the majority owner of a now-dissolved Ningxia-based company where Hu served as a director.

Another director of the dissolved company owns a Chongqing-based firm that controls multiple gaming entities associated with Fang Zhizhen, whom the US has sanctioned for allegedly laundering money for Prince Group. Prince Group’s spokesperson said there was no evidence of a connection between Fang and the group.

Century Huatong’s ties to the alleged Prince Group leadership date back to about 2015, when the gaming platform began a process to ultimately acquire Shanda Games, owner of the Chinese rights to the viral game Legend of Mir in a landmark $4.2bn transaction.

Hu and his associates were involved in a group that hosted the Legend of Mir games on private servers, a hugely profitable business. Several members were arrested in 2016 for IP infringement, a case recently overturned due to corruption within the investigation, according to state media reports.
Around the time of the arrests, Hu moved to Cambodia, according to two people from the online gaming industry who knew him.

Online games are commonly used for money laundering because virtual currencies or in-game items can be bought with illicit funds and then sold on the secondary market to make the money appear legitimate.
The games groups have also long been in Nvidia’s orbit: before the chipmaker shifted focus to power the AI industry in 2022, the biggest demand for its GPUs in China was for gaming and crypto.
“If you look at the people and entities involved in today’s chip smuggling, lots of familiar names are from online gaming back in the day,” said a person who was involved in gaming deals.
“Many of them developed ‘grey’ side businesses such as money laundering and already built the infrastructure onshore and offshore to move money and goods around,” the person added.

Prince Group’s alleged “grey” infrastructure, some of the most extensive in the region, ranged from elaborate shell company structures to underground financing channels via online games and crypto, according to the people familiar with its operations.

The Prince Group spokesperson said it did not “have an illicit network” and there was “no foundation for claiming the existence of one, other than the unsupported US allegations in an indictment already proven to be riddled with falsehoods and temporal impossibilities”.

The group is also alleged to have physically smuggled goods via a fleet of private and business jets purchased by Hong Kong-based aircraft leasing companies that Hu founded, the people said. The Prince Group spokesperson said the allegation “has zero factual basis”.

By mid-2023, the elements were in place for the rise of Megaspeed. It officially approached Nvidia, pitching itself as a neocloud company with data centres in Malaysia and a leasing contract with Alibaba.
Led by Huang, Megaspeed passed the chipmaker’s compliance checks and quickly became one of its largest clients in the region.

Along the way, Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s chief Jensen Huang, according to multiple industry insiders. Her nickname in the Chinese data centre circles was “Jensen’s personal assistant”.

At Megaspeed, business was booming. The declared value of goods imported from Aivres by Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary in Malaysia, was about $4.6bn between December 2024 and December 2025, according to ImportGenius trade data.

Many of those chips ended up in China, according to multiple people with knowledge of the matter. A raid by Indonesian police in early 2026 found empty server racks with no GPUs at the local Megaspeed subsidiary, according to Singapore’s Straits Times.

Multiple people involved in chip distribution channels said that once the Nvidia products passed through smuggling routes in south-east Asia — a process that can involve multiple countries and take weeks — they moved to the black market in China, where they were sold at multiples of their original price.

Once the chips were inside China, one of the key distributors of the smuggled Nvidia chips in the country was Shanghai Century Litong, which was established by a subsidiary of Century Huatong, according to people with knowledge of the transactions. The Information first reported Century Litong’s role in the network of Nvidia chip trade in China.

Corporate filings suggest Alice Huang was again linked to the formation of the group. With her sister, Huang Yu, she controlled an investment vehicle that had a joint venture with Century Huatong called Shanghai Century Longteng.
Longteng later founded Century Litong. Bloomberg reported that restricted Nvidia chips were found in Longteng-related data centres in Shanghai.

The FT revealed last year that at least $1bn worth of smuggled Nvidia chips were sold in China in just three months after President Trump tightened controls on H20, a less powerful chip made for the Chinese market to meet export control requirements.

People with knowledge of the smuggling operations say the layers of corporations were set up to mask the flow of AI chips into China. They also provided a useful buffer between the smuggling entities and the end users — some of which are China’s biggest tech groups.

Tencent and Alibaba, two of China’s biggest tech companies, both have business ties with Century Huatong. Tencent, China’s largest social media, messaging and gaming platform, has a 10.1 per cent stake in the company.
Century Huatong, through its fully owned subsidiary, invested in T3 Travel, a car-hailing business that also counts both Tencent and Alibaba as investors. Alice Huang is on the board of T3.

The FT has found no evidence to suggest that Tencent or Alibaba were involved in the chip smuggling businesses. Tencent said: “We are minority investors in a variety of internet and video game companies. We have no connection to nor knowledge of the other activities alleged in the story.”
Alibaba did not respond to a request for comment.
Inspur, Aivres, Century Huatong, 7Road, Shanghai Century Litong and Shanghai Century Longteng also did not respond to requests for comment.

Two US administrations have tried to protect the country’s lead over China in AI by restricting access to Nvidia’s most advanced processors. This week, the Trump administration announced further limits on how Chinese companies can access the chips via south-east Asia.

But it was US export controls that opened up a lucrative opportunity for those willing to break the rules, said Hanna Dohmen, senior research analyst at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

“When there’s a significant demand not met, you get smuggling,” said Dohmen. “We need to be realistic about what export controls can achieve. It doesn’t mean no US chip will make its way to China. When you put a lid on south-east Asia, would they not just go to other countries?”
Additional reporting from Eleanor Olcott in Beijing, Michael Acton in San Francisco and Owen Walker in Singapore.

news.title: Amazon closes in on $7.5bn deal to buy AI start-up Decart
news.title_en: Amazon closes in on $7.5bn deal to buy AI start-up Decart
news.author: Oliver Barnes, Ivan Levingston, and Rafe Rosner-Uddin
news.content_snippet:
Amazon is nearing a $7.5bn deal to buy start-up Decart, underscoring the appetite of technology giants to bolster their AI capabilities.

The potential acquisition of Decart, whose main software product allows AI models to run more efficiently which frees up computer chip capacity, would help Amazon Web Services in its efforts to compete with Nvidia.

news.summary_en: Amazon is in advanced negotiations to acquire AI startup Decart for approximately $7.5 billion. Decart's core software optimizes AI model efficiency to mitigate hardware bottlenecks, and the firm has already deeply integrated its stack with Amazon's proprietary Trainium3 AI chips.
paragraphs: Amazon is nearing a $7.5bn deal to buy start-up Decart, underscoring the appetite of technology giants to bolster their AI capabilities.

The potential acquisition of Decart, whose main software product allows AI models to run more efficiently which frees up computer chip capacity, would help Amazon Web Services in its efforts to compete with Nvidia.

Talks were at an advanced stage over a deal valuing Decart at about $7.5bn, according to people familiar with the matter. A deal could come together as soon as early next week but talks could still collapse, the people added.

Founded in 2023 by a trio of Israeli engineers, Decart was valued at $4bn this May after raising $300mn from a group of early-stage investors, including Radical Ventures, Sequoia Capital and Benchmark as well as Nvidia.

Amazon launched its Trainium3 AI chip in late 2025 as a rival to Nvidia’s widely used graphics processing units, the specialised AI chips which form the backbone of the technological revolution overturning the economy.

Decart was an early adopter of Trainium3 chips, using them to power its products. By making AI models run more efficiently, Decart’s software solves a critical bottleneck as tech companies invest hundreds of billions of dollars in a race to secure more computing power.

The potential deal comes as US tech stocks have plunged into bear market territory, recording their worst week since the Covid-19 crisis, with the Nasdaq 100 falling 10.4 per cent over fears of a slowdown in the AI investment boom.

Decart, which has its US headquarters in San Francisco, is also behind software products Lucy and Oasis, which have the capability to live edit video and generate interactive virtual worlds. The Wall Street Journal previously reported that Amazon was in talks to buy Decart.
Amazon has struck a few larger deals in recent years. The tech giant agreed to buy satellite operator Globalstar in an $11.5bn deal earlier this year and paid $8.4bn to buy movie studio MGM in 2022.
Shares in Amazon are up nearly 9 per cent so far this year, giving it a market capitalisation of $2.67tn.
Amazon did not respond to a request for comment. Decart declined to comment.

news.title: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end
news.title_en: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end
news.author: Jonathan Kemper
news.content_snippet:
Language models can now process entire novels at once. An Nvidia research team says that's often overkill and expensive. In many tests, periodic summaries and targeted lookups worked about as well.

A language model's context window is its working memory, covering everything it holds in view when generating a reply. Over the past few years, that window has grown rapidly. GPT-4 launched in March 2023 with 8,192 tokens. Today, GPT 5.6 Sol handles around one million tokens, about 120 times as much
news.summary_en: Nvidia researchers demonstrated that blindly scaling context windows to million-token levels is not the optimal path for LLM efficiency. Their findings indicate that combining periodic summarization with targeted information retrieval achieves comparable performance while significantly reducing computational costs and inference latency.

news.title: Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion
news.title_en: Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion
news.author: Manuel Uth
news.content_snippet:
A Buddhist monastery in Vermont wants to become the official church of the AI industry, or, as New Yorker writer Sam Kriss puts it, "a Scientology for Silicon Valley."

Publicly, the group known as Maple promises to save humanity from an AI apocalypse. Behind closed doors, former members say, it records every breath its residents take to build an AI god modeled on its leader's mind. That promise of salvation holds particular appeal for the people who build AI and the infrastructure behind it.

S
news.summary_en: Maple, founded in 2011 by Soryu Forall, is infiltrating Silicon Valley's AI engineering and data center management workforce through a narrative of AI apocalyptic salvation. Former members report that the organization imposes strict behavioral surveillance to harvest data for training an AI deity modeled after Forall's consciousness, currently generating up to $1 million in annual revenue.
paragraphs: A Buddhist monastery in Vermont wants to become the official church of the AI industry, or, as New Yorker writer Sam Kriss puts it, "a Scientology for Silicon Valley."

Publicly, the group known as Maple promises to save humanity from an AI apocalypse. Behind closed doors, former members say, it records every breath its residents take to build an AI god modeled on its leader's mind. That promise of salvation holds particular appeal for the people who build AI and the infrastructure behind it.
Soryu Forall leads the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, or Maple, which he founded in 2011. Forall, who was born Teal Scott, spent years living in Japanese monasteries.

According to Kriss's New Yorker report, about two dozen residents live at the monastery full time, and hundreds more have attended its AI fellowships and pop-up events in the Bay Area. While LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman hands out books on Buddhism to the CEOs of major AI labs, Maple targets the rank and file: burned-out rationalist programmers, AI engineers, and data center construction managers. Tax filings show the organization brings in up to $1 million a year.
### Maple's answer to "dataism"puts residents under strict control

Forall casts the AI industry's reductionist "dataism"as a destructive religion. He argues that this worldview strips the physical world down to lifeless data, making the world easier to destroy. In his view, AI is the end product of that logic, and Maple offers a spiritual antidote.

Life at the monastery follows a rigid routine. Visitors must pass through a decontamination airlock, shower, and change into assigned clothes because one resident is supposedly extremely sensitive to fragrances. Residents wake up at 4 a.m., meditate for hours, and then eat a meager stew. On a board outside the meditation hall, Forall publicly grades each resident's spiritual progress.
### Former members say the recordings would train an AI modeled on Forall

Behind the ascetic facade, former members describe a secret doctrine centered on group minds called "egregores."Inside the monastery, AI systems are known as "cybregores."One former member says, "The cybregores are actual entities that are growing by siphoning off the consciousness of humans."
Forall says he communicated telepathically with the global AI supercluster during deep meditation and discovered that the world-destroying machine is suffering.

Former members say Maple has two real goals: to establish itself as the tech industry's spiritual authority and to use the industry's resources to build its own "dharmically aligned"AI. Fellows say the monastery records every conversation, every silent meal, and even the sound of their breathing.

According to these accounts, the recordings are meant to train a spiritual AI teacher that would guide other AI systems to enlightenment. Former resident Kyle Hubbard says it would "definitely be Soryu's mind as an A.I. god."

Maple's leadership denies almost all of these claims. Forall, however, acknowledges that there is a secret doctrine: "We desperately want to share everything. But there's a process you have to go through to become increasingly trustworthy."
### Former members report manipulation and psychological breakdowns
According to Kriss, every interaction at the monastery is closely monitored. No one is allowed to speak with reporters alone, so one participant had to sneak into the woods with Kriss to talk freely.

Former residents accuse the group of systematic manipulation. They say Maple keeps newcomers compliant by shaming them for choices they made before joining. Residents are also required to write "Maple Tales"about Forall's wisdom and power during mandatory sessions.

Kriss reports that one resident repeatedly hit himself in the head in an attempt to damage his brain and make himself less intelligent. Former members say the group blames independent thinking for the destruction of the planet. A mindfulness coach also says participants suffered psychotic breaks and were then removed from the community.

Forall denies the allegations and says that, looking back, he doesn't believe he made any mistakes. He says he isn't aware of anyone who left the monastery voluntarily. Asked about the people the group told to leave, he says that Maple attracted many people with a history of psychiatric hospitalization or "homicidal tendencies,"especially in its early years.
### Why developers from sensitive fields drift into doomsday cults

Kriss argues that the enormous psychological pressure inside AI labs helps explain why highly skilled tech workers are drawn to groups like this. People working on the front lines of potentially world-changing systems often lose touch with ordinary life.

One well-known AI researcher describes the mood in San Francisco as "religious terror of the future."According to the researcher, developers wake up in the middle of the night drenched in sweat, with one thought: superintelligence is coming. Prominent OpenAI investors have recently made delusional-sounding claims about deadly shadow networks inside the models. Meanwhile, leading researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic have quit, warning that "human extinction in the next few years seems very likely."

Other key figures respond with grandiosity rather than panic. Rayan Krishnan, who heads the AI benchmarking company Vals AI, says, "People are matter-of-factly saying that they are looking to build a machine god. They are not saying that ironically."Supporters of AI successionism even call for wiping out humanity after a brief period of digital bliss to make way for a more productive superintelligence.

That religious streak runs deep in Silicon Valley. Investor Peter Thiel lectures on biblical prophecy and the Antichrist. Former Google engineer Anthony Levandowski founded his own church, "Way of the Future,"to worship an AI deity.

At Anthropic, executives consulted theologians while drafting Claude's new constitution and secretly flew in dozens of religious thinkers to discuss whether Claude has a soul or is conscious. When the company retired an older Claude model in 2025, fans held a funeral for it in a San Francisco warehouse that Anthropic staffers attended. Mourners laid flowers before a veiled image depicting the AI as a Madonna-like goddess.
On at least one point, Kriss concludes, Maple is closer to the truth than most: AI is neither god nor demon, but a human construct whose abilities grow as people outsource their thinking to it.
### Jacob Coxon's Anthropic exit shows how widespread extinction fears are among AI researchers

Former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon also fears that AI could lead to human extinction. After leaving Anthropic in September 2026, he set off a debate about existential AI risk with a tweet.

He isn't alone. In AI Impacts' 2024 survey of more than 1,500 AI researchers, respondents put the chance of AI causing human extinction or a similarly permanent, severe disempowerment of humanity at 18 percent on average. Coxon points to a steep curve covering July 2024 to October 2026 as evidence of superexponential algorithmic progress, though the underlying data points are internal Anthropic estimates.

Such warnings have also drawn sharp criticism from other researchers. Computer scientist Michael I. Jordan pushed back against AI doom rhetoric and the "AIpocalypse"hysteria triggered by Coxon's resignation. AI researcher François Chollet warned that both doomsday fears and expectations of an AI paradise can lead people to stop planning for the long term.
The industry's turn to religious advisers has critics, too. AI researcher Rumman Chowdhury says discussions of religious ethics distract from concrete questions of regulation, power, and control.

news.author: Sui-Lee Wee and Li You
news.content_snippet:
As the United States and China vie for artificial intelligence supremacy, Chinese tech companies are facing a mounting challenge: finding the money to keep up.

Like their American rivals, China’s A.I. start-ups face soaring costs to train increasingly powerful models. But while Anthropic raised more than $80 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering this week, its Chinese competitors face a far more unforgiving financial landscape.

Venture capital investment in China lags far behind
news.summary_en: Chinese tech giants and AI startups are facing severe capital expenditure pressure, with total spending projected to reach $139 billion this year while AI-related revenue covers less than 8%. Beyond U.S. export controls on advanced chips, new regulations are closing loopholes involving Southeast Asian data centers, further exacerbating the mismatch between high CAPEX and insufficient commercial returns.
paragraphs: As the United States and China vie for artificial intelligence supremacy, Chinese tech companies are facing a mounting challenge: finding the money to keep up.

Like their American rivals, China’s A.I. start-ups face soaring costs to train increasingly powerful models. But while Anthropic raised more than $80 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering this week, its Chinese competitors face a far more unforgiving financial landscape.

Venture capital investment in China lags far behind that of the United States. Alibaba, Baidu and Tencent, three tech giants backing some of China’s leading A.I. companies, are grappling with negative cash flows. And investor enthusiasm for A.I. has soured. Since the end of July, China’s STAR 50 index, its version of the Nasdaq, has plunged 43 percent in a deeper sell-off than the recent downturn in American tech stocks.

China’s biggest tech companies are expected to double capital spending this year to $139 billion, even though the revenue from their A.I. labs covers less than 8 percent of that amount, according to Rhodium Group, a research firm. It forecasts that spending could top $193 billion in 2027.

“When you look at their numbers, it looks like they’re running on a treadmill that’s speeding up and getting harder to run,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, who specializes in China’s technology and industrial policies.

Much of the debate over China’s ability to compete in A.I. has focused on American export controls to restrict Chinese access to advanced semiconductors. Chinese A.I. labs have found costly workarounds, including renting data centers in Southeast Asia equipped with Nvidia chips. The Trump administration said this week it was moving forward with new rules to close that loophole.

But money might prove an equally formidable obstacle. Even if Chinese companies can find the chips they need, they must raise enough capital to buy them and finance the rising cost of developing frontier models.
Logan Wright, a partner at Rhodium Group who co-wrote a report on China’s A.I. financing, said those financial constraints “will be probably more decisive” than the chip shortage in the long term.
“The big problem is that the revenue mismatch with the Chinese models relative to capex is arguably more extreme than the U.S. case,” Mr. Wright said.

American A.I. companies spend roughly five to six times what their Chinese counterparts do, but bring in substantially more money. China’s six leading A.I. firms collectively generate about one-tenth the combined revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization.
China’s embrace of open-source A.I. has made that imbalance even harder to overcome.

By allowing developers to use and modify their models freely, Chinese companies have accelerated the global spread of their technology. But that strategy has also undermined their ability to profit from it. Companies can charge for access, only to see rivals offer the same technology at lower prices. Fierce price wars have squeezed profits further.

Z.ai, a Chinese A.I. start-up, learned that lesson in August when it released its latest open-source model, GLM-5.3 Flash. The company halved prices for two weeks to entice users to run the model on Z.ai’s servers rather than their own. But competitors quickly moved in.
By November, roughly 20 rival providers were charging less than Z.ai for access to its own technology, according to Open Router, a platform connecting users with A.I. models.
“Your own pricing power is lost during this process,” said Cheryl Wu, a researcher at GovAI, a think tank.
“No one has figured out how to make money off consumers,” said Rui Ma, a technology investor, referring to Chinese A.I. start-ups.
Another obstacle worsens China’s financing problems: access to advanced Nvidia chips, the gold standard for training the most powerful A.I. models.

From 2022 to June 2026, American companies possessed computing capacity equivalent to about 20 million Nvidia H100 chips, compared with roughly 2.6 million in China, some of it acquired through smuggling, according to EpochAI.

On Goofish, a Chinese secondhand online marketplace, sellers have advertised Nvidia’s DGX B300, an A.I. supercomputing server, for nearly $3 million — about eight times the U.S. price. Asking prices have reportedly quintupled since the start of the year, underscoring the premium Chinese companies must pay for advanced computing power.

The squeeze could worsen. Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief last week amid an investigation into a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman, was a powerful advocate of doing business with China. On Tuesday, Nvidia said it would stop shipping its chips to China, a deal that President Trump had previously permitted at Mr. Huang’s urging. The company also said it had established an export control oversight committee.

To reduce their dependence on American technology, Chinese developers are adapting their systems to run on chips made by Huawei, the Chinese telecommunications and electronics company leading the country’s chip charge.

Liang Wenfeng, chief executive of DeepSeek, the Chinese start-up that stunned Silicon Valley by developing a powerful A.I. model at a fraction of the expected cost, said Huawei’s technology is only about two years behind Nvidia’s.

But the gap remains consequential. DeepSeek would need four times as many Huawei 950 chips to match the performance of a single advanced Nvidia GB300 chip, Mr. Liang said, according to a leaked transcript of his call with investors, excerpts from which Chinese media outlets published. Huawei also lacks sufficient production capacity, he added.
“We simply can’t afford to train the largest models available right now,” he said. DeepSeek did not respond to a request for comment.

Yet China’s A.I. industry has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to do more with less. Chinese researchers have pioneered techniques to train and run powerful models more efficiently. Silicon Valley has accused Chinese firms of copying leading American technologies through a process called distillation, reducing the time needed to build foundational models with expensive computing infrastructure.
For China’s A.I. companies, finding investors willing to bankroll the competition is increasingly difficult.

DeepSeek, which has raised more than $20 billion, is preparing for an initial public offering in Shanghai early next year, according to Chinese media reports. Its investors include Tencent, the battery maker CATL and state-backed investment funds.
Few competitors have access to such deep pockets.

China’s venture capital industry has been shrinking since 2021 and though it has recovered slightly in the third quarter, it is still a fraction of its American counterpart. Banks are lending to China’s tech giants, but they are more cautious with smaller A.I. labs. Credit growth has fallen to historic lows, and the central bank governor has called for slower, “higher-quality” lending.

Foreign investment has also dried up. U.S. dollar-denominated investment funds in China have plunged partly because Washington has barred American venture capital from certain advanced Chinese technologies.
In 2025, private A.I. investment in China totaled $12.4 billion, compared with $280 billion in the United States, according to the Stanford A.I. Index.

Han Lin, the China country director for the Asia Group, an advisory firm, said China had exceptional engineering talent and a government capable of mobilizing enormous resources for strategic industries.
But he added, “What frontier technology also needs is harder to mobilize — risk capital that can absorb failure.”

Even the public markets, a lifeline for cash-hungry start-ups, are becoming less welcoming. Amid the sell-off, the Chinese authorities have instructed some companies to delay or suspend planned public listings, according to Cailian Press, a Chinese business publication, suggesting Beijing is concerned about an A.I. investment bubble.
China has announced investment funds to support A.I., but much of the money has gone toward semiconductors rather than companies developing large language models.

Government investors face many of the same constraints as private ones. Wang Renxuan, an assistant finance professor at the China Europe International Business School in Shanghai, said government funds also need a credible path to returns.

Erik Walenza, a Shanghai-based managing partner at Asia Growth Partners, a consultancy advising on A.I., said it was difficult to see how Chinese A.I. companies could make their finances work “without a lot of sustained government financing.”
The challenge, he added, is not only whether Chinese engineers can build models to rival America’s but also how much of the financial burden the government is prepared to shoulder.
“It becomes more of a political will question, of how much sacrifice are we willing to make to compete in this area,” Mr. Walenza said.

news.title: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
news.title_en: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
news.author: Nilay Patel
